summary_html: Cases arising on **federal lands/facilities** or involving **Indian children** invoke federal/tribal jurisdictional rules (VICAA for federal facilities; **ICWA** for Indian children and tribal preference/jurisdiction).
authority_html:
- **VICAA (34 U.S.C. §§ 20301–20307)** — federal-facility reporting mandates  
- **ICWA (25 U.S.C. §§ 1901–1963)** — tribal jurisdiction, placement preferences, notice to tribes

primary_citations.citation_text: Montana - Title 41, Chapter 3 (Child Abuse and Neglect – mandatory reporting and protective services)

regulations_applicable.title: Department 37 - PUBLIC HEALTH AND HUMAN SERVICES

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians v. Holyfield
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: ICWA's term 'domicile' has a uniform federal meaning; twins born off-reservation to reservation-domiciled parents were themselves domiciled on the reservation, so 25 U.S.C. § 1911(a) vested exclusive jurisdiction in the tribal court and the state adoption decree was vacated.
key_cases.relevance: It is the Supreme Court's controlling decision on when a Montana district court has no jurisdiction at all because the Indian child is domiciled on a reservation.
key_cases.quote: In enacting the ICWA Congress confirmed that, in child custody proceedings involving Indian children domiciled on the reservation, tribal jurisdiction was exclusive as to the States.

key_cases.holding: The district court abused its discretion by terminating parental rights without a conclusive tribal determination of the child's membership or eligibility where, for eighteen months, the court and parties had reason to believe the child might be an Indian child; the Department's passive reliance on the tribe's inaction and the parents' beliefs did not satisfy its ICWA burden.
key_cases.relevance: It imposes an affirmative duty on the Department to ask, actively investigate and obtain a conclusive tribal determination whenever there is reason to believe a child may be an Indian child.
key_cases.quote: Contrary to the State's assertion, a parent cannot waive application of ICWA by stipulation or acquiescence.

key_cases.holding: Termination was reversed and remanded for a new hearing because the record did not substantiate ten-day ICWA notice to the mother and the tribe, the ICWA qualified expert did not testify that continued custody was likely to result in serious emotional or physical damage, and the court made no findings on active efforts.
key_cases.relevance: It is the Montana Supreme Court's enforcement decision on the three operative ICWA duties — notice, qualified expert testimony and active efforts — and it holds that active efforts must be shown beyond a reasonable doubt.
key_cases.quote: ICWA sets minimum federal standards for proceedings involving Indian children, and we are compelled to make sure its requirements are followed.

key_cases.holding: Termination of a putative father's rights to an Indian child was affirmed without active-efforts proof or qualified expert testimony because, under Adoptive Couple v. Baby Girl, 25 U.S.C. § 1912(d) and (f) do not apply where the parent never had custody and no Indian family relationship existed to break up.
key_cases.relevance: It marks the outer limit of ICWA's § 1912 protections in Montana: a putative father who never had custody and never established a relationship cannot invoke active efforts or the qualified-expert requirement.
key_cases.quote: Although the District Court order does not comply with ICWA requirements, the § 1912 ICWA provisions do not apply because a family relationship does not exist.

key_cases.holding: An order adjudicating two Indian children youths in need of care and granting DPHHS temporary legal custody was affirmed: as a matter of first impression, the evidentiary standard for ICWA 'active efforts' under 25 U.S.C. § 1912(d) matches the underlying proceeding — clear and convincing evidence where the proceeding is foster-care placement under § 1912(e), and proof beyond a reasonable doubt where it is termination under § 1912(f).
key_cases.relevance: It is the source of Montana's ICWA active-efforts burden of proof, and it shows the rule is tiered — beyond a reasonable doubt only when the underlying proceeding is termination, clear and convincing evidence for foster-care placement.
key_cases.quote: we conclude that the proper evidentiary standard for determining "active efforts" under § 1912(d) is the same standard we apply to the underlying ICWA proceeding

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The South Carolina judgment awarding custody to the biological father was reversed: 25 U.S.C. § 1912(f) does not apply where the Indian parent never had custody of the Indian child, § 1912(d)'s remedial-efforts requirement is inapplicable where the parent abandoned the child before birth and never had custody, and § 1915(a)'s placement preferences do not bar a non-Indian adoption when no other eligible candidate has sought to adopt.
key_cases.relevance: It is the Supreme Court holding on which Montana's In re P.T.D. and In re J.S. entirely turn, and it marks the outer boundary of ICWA's § 1912 protections where the parent never had custody of the child.
key_cases.quote: §1912(f) does not apply in cases where the Indian parent never had custody of the Indian child

search_keywords: Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services

state_agency.name: Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services, Child and Family Services Division

mandatory_reporters: Physicians, residents, interns, and hospital staff engaged in the admission, examination, care, or treatment of persons — Mont. Code Ann. § 41-3-201(2)(a)
Nurses, osteopaths, chiropractors, podiatrists, medical examiners, coroners, dentists, optometrists, and any other health or mental health professionals — Mont. Code Ann. § 41-3-201(2)(b)
School teachers, other school officials, and employees who work during regular school hours — Mont. Code Ann. § 41-3-201(2)(d)

Social workers licensed pursuant to Title 37, child protection investigators, child reunification specialists, operators or employees of any registered or licensed day-care or substitute care facility, staff of a resource and referral grant program organized under § 52-2-711 or of a child and adult food care program, and operators or employees of a child-care facility — Mont. Code Ann. § 41-3-201(2)(e)
Foster care, residential, and institutional workers — Mont. Code Ann. § 41-3-201(2)(f)
Peace officers and other law enforcement officials — Mont. Code Ann. § 41-3-201(2)(g)
Members of the clergy, subject to the confessional and canon-law exceptions — Mont. Code Ann. § 41-3-201(2)(h), (6)(b)–(c)
Guardians ad litem and court-appointed advocates authorized to investigate a report of alleged abuse or neglect — Mont. Code Ann. § 41-3-201(2)(i)
Employees of entities that contract with the department to provide direct services to children — Mont. Code Ann. § 41-3-201(2)(j)
Department employees while in the conduct of their duties — Mont. Code Ann. § 41-3-201(2)(k)

Added duty: a professional listed in § 41-3-201(2)(a) or (2)(b) who is involved in the delivery or care of an infant must report any infant known to the professional to be affected by a dangerous drug, as defined in § 50-32-101 — Mont. Code Ann. § 41-3-201(3)
reporting_details: Montana is not a universal-reporter state: only the professionals and officials listed in Mont. Code Ann. § 41-3-201(2) must report promptly to the department when, in their professional or official capacity, they know or have reasonable cause to suspect a child is abused or neglected, while § 41-3-201(4) allows any other person to report voluntarily.

timeline_requirements.requirement_name: Written safety and risk assessment furnished
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Statute states no penalty; within 60 days the child protection investigator must furnish the written safety and risk assessment to the department and, on request, to the family (Mont. Code Ann. § 41-3-202(6))
